Area Of Triangle

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: Move a triangle and watch the rectangles built on its base: the triangle always takes exactly half of the big rectangle. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the triangle, the point names or the coloured rectangles.

Drag a corner, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

The triangle inside the rectangle seems to take up half of it, and it keeps doing so however you drag the corners. Here is why, including the cases where the top corner sits outside the bottom side.

Half of the box

Drop the top corner C straight down to H on the bottom side AB. The dashed line CH is the altitude, and ABQP is the rectangle on base AB with that same height. Its area is base × altitude. The page's claim is that the triangle takes exactly half of that rectangle:

Area(ABC) = Area(ABQP) / 2

The logic test checked this for 529 grid triangles plus 500 random ones, with H inside the base, beyond either end, and on the base line. It held every time, just as the original page says.

Two rectangles that add up

Beside ABQP lie AHCP on the piece AH and HBQC on the piece HB. Their widths are signed: when H lies between A and B both are ordinary widths and the two small rectangles are parts of the big one. When H lies outside AB, one width is negative, so that rectangle is counted with a minus sign. Either way the page's equality holds:

Area(ABQP) = Area(AHCP) + Area(HBQC)

Multiply the signed widths AH and HB by the same altitude CH. Since AH + HB = AB along the base line, the two areas always add up to the area of ABQP. The test compared this equality with a direct calculation of all three rectangles over the whole grid; it never failed, including the outside cases that many school treatments leave out.

The parallelogram and Euclid

There is a second way to see the half. Turn the triangle through 180 degrees about the middle of any side: the copy and the original make a parallelogram with the same base and altitude, so its area is base × altitude — twice the triangle. The test did this for all three sides of every triangle in the grid and the random sample. This is the reasoning behind Euclid I.37 in the Elements: triangles with the same base and altitude have equal areas.

Try dragging C past A or past B so that H leaves the base: one coloured rectangle flips its sign, but the numbers in the status line still add up.
